lessons.title: Technique reset
lessons.focus: Set up the guitar comfortably, identify the six strings and tune to standard pitch.
learningObjectives: Name the six strings from low to high (E–A–D–G–B–E) and describe the standard tuning targets.
Tune each string individually with a tuner, then recheck the full set after the first pass.
Demonstrate a supported seated or standing setup that lets both hands move without gripping or avoidable strain.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: A stable setup lets the hands focus on sound and movement instead of holding the instrument in place. Tuning is a comparison task: adjust one string toward its target, then recheck all six because changing string tension can slightly affect the others.
explanation.plainLanguage: Support the guitar with your body or strap, not with a tight fretting-hand grip. Tune one string at a time using small peg movements, then check the whole set again.
explanation.workedExample: Standard tuning check: from thickest to thinnest string, E2–A2–D3–G3–B3–E4. Use the tuner to verify each open string, then say the note names without looking.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a tuner display set to standard E–A–D–G–B–E and observe the learner's own comfortable instrument support. Do not treat one seated or standing posture as a universal body template.
steps: Support the guitar on your leg or with the strap so it stays in place without being held by the fretting hand.
Relax the shoulders and wrists; check that both hands can reach their normal playing areas without forcing the joint angle.
Name the strings from thickest to thinnest: low E, A, D, G, B, high E.
Set the tuner to standard tuning. Pluck one open string at a time and make small peg adjustments toward its target note.
Repeat the check from low E to high E after the first pass; retune any string that moved while the others were adjusted.
Play each open string once, listen for a stable pitch, and repeat the setup without reading the string list.

instructions: Place the guitar in your usual seated or standing position.

exercises.successCriterion: The learner names E–A–D–G–B–E in order and can adjust the instrument support without creating discomfort.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Tune low E, A, D, G, B and high E one at a time using small peg movements.

exercises.title: Musical application
instructions: Begin with the guitar already supported comfortably.

exercises.successCriterion: The learner completes the setup and tuning sequence independently, names the strings in order and keeps the instrument supported while playing.

instructions: Put the string chart away and recall the six strings in order.

lessons.title: Pentatonic across neck
lessons.focus: Connect two A minor pentatonic positions across the neck and compare their five notes with the C major scale.
learningObjectives: Play a short C major pattern and state its whole-step/half-step formula; identify how A minor pentatonic uses A–C–D–E–G.
Play A minor pentatonic box 1 and the adjacent box 2, naming the five notes and locating A as the tonal centre.
Create a short call-and-response phrase that moves between the two positions and resolves deliberately to A.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: The C major scale contains C–D–E–F–G–A–B. A minor pentatonic uses five notes from that same note collection—A, C, D, E and G—leaving out B and F. Two neighbouring fretboard positions let you keep the same musical idea while moving across the neck.
explanation.plainLanguage: Learn the five notes first, then find them in two nearby fretboard shapes. The shapes are maps of the same A minor pentatonic sound, not two different scales. Finish phrases on A so the tonal centre remains clear.
explanation.workedExample: A minor pentatonic box 1: low E 5–8, A 5–7, D 5–7, G 5–7, B 5–8, high e 5–8. Adjacent box 2: low E 8–10, A 7–10, D 7–10, G 7–9, B 8–10, high e 8–10.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a clear fretboard diagram showing A minor pentatonic box 1 at the fifth position and the adjacent box 2, with A-root notes highlighted. Demonstrate the shift slowly before adding a backing track.
steps: Play C major slowly and say the notes C–D–E–F–G–A–B; recall the formula whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half.
Compare the note collection with A minor pentatonic: A–C–D–E–G. Say which two C-major notes are left out.
Play box 1 at the fifth position: low E 5–8, A 5–7, D 5–7, G 5–7, B 5–8, high e 5–8.
Play the adjacent box 2: low E 8–10, A 7–10, D 7–10, G 7–9, B 8–10, high e 8–10.
Connect the shapes slowly through the shared notes around the seventh-to-eighth-fret area; name A whenever you reach a root note.
Create a two-bar question and answer. Use notes from both positions and leave the final note on A.

lessons.title: Bends to pitch
lessons.focus: Bend a target pitch accurately and shape a short A minor pentatonic phrase over a blues pulse.
learningObjectives: Locate the G starting note and A target note on the B string, and compare the target with a fretted reference pitch.
Bend B-string fret 8 (G) up a whole step to match fret 10 (A), sustain it briefly and release with control.
Use one controlled bend in a short A minor pentatonic phrase, leaving musical space and maintaining the pulse.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: A bend raises a fretted note by increasing string tension. The target pitch should be heard and checked against a known reference note; the bend is not complete just because the string has moved. Support the bending finger, stop at the intended pitch and release without dropping the pulse.
explanation.plainLanguage: Play the note you want to reach first. Then fret the lower note and bend it until it sounds like that target. Keep the movement controlled, listen for the pitch and let the note return smoothly.
explanation.workedExample: On the B string, fret 10 and hear A. Fret 8 (G), bend it up one whole step until it matches the A reference, hold briefly and release to G. Use the bend once in a short A minor pentatonic phrase.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a close-up demonstration on the B string that first sounds the target A at fret 10, then bends G at fret 8 to match it. A tuner may support checking, but listening to the fretted reference is part of the task.
steps: On the B string, play fret 10 and listen carefully to the target A pitch.
Play fret 8 (G) on the same string, then bend it upward slowly until it matches the fretted A reference.
Use the index and middle fingers behind the bending finger for support; keep the wrist and thumb comfortable.
Hold the target briefly, release smoothly to G and compare the returned note with the original starting pitch.
Repeat at a slow pulse. If a whole-step bend is uncomfortable, use a smaller interval and compare it with the matching fretted target.
Place one controlled bend into a short A minor pentatonic phrase over an A blues pulse; leave space before the next idea.

lessons.title: Legato control
lessons.focus: Coordinate alternate picking, clean two-string crossings and legato articulation with even timing and volume.
learningObjectives: Play a down-up picking sequence on one string and preserve the sequence when moving to a neighbouring string.
Cross from the D string to the G string with planned pick directions and without unintended string noise.
Perform a B-string hammer-on/pull-off cell without re-picking each note, keeping timing and volume even.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: Alternate picking uses a planned down-up sequence. String crossing means carrying that sequence to the next string without resetting automatically. Legato uses fretting-hand movement—such as hammer-ons and pull-offs—to sound connected notes without picking every pitch. These are related but distinct skills and need separate checks.
explanation.plainLanguage: Practise the picking pattern and the legato pattern separately first. Keep the pick moving down-up as you cross strings. For legato, pick the first note, hammer to the higher fret, pull back and hammer again without extra pick strokes.
explanation.workedExample: Picking: D string 5–7 then G string 5–7 with down-up-down-up. Legato: B string 5–7–5–7—pick fret 5, hammer to 7, pull to 5, then hammer to 7.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Show a close-up picking-hand view for the D-to-G string crossing and a fretting-hand view for the B-string 5–7–5–7 legato cell. Demonstrate each movement separately before combining them.
steps: Hold the pick without a rigid grip and expose only enough tip to contact the string.
On the D string, play frets 5 and 7 using down then up strokes.
Continue to the G string at frets 5 and 7, preserving the next down-up strokes rather than restarting the pattern.
Play the picking cell slowly and listen for even timing and attack across the string change.
On the B string, pick fret 5, hammer to fret 7, pull back to fret 5 and hammer to fret 7; do not pick each legato note.
Compare the timing and volume of the four legato notes, then join the picking and legato cells in a short phrase.
